notes.meaning: Joab receives a report that King David is weeping and grieving deeply for his son Absalom. Instead of celebrating the victory that saved his life and his kingdom, the king is swallowed up by personal sorrow. His mourning shows how heavily the loss of his son weighed on him.

The joy of that day's triumph quickly turns into sadness for the entire army. When the soldiers hear how brokenhearted the king is, their own excitement fades away. They feel guilty and downcast rather than proud of saving the realm.

The soldiers sneak back into the city of Mahanaim quietly instead of marching in with songs of victory. They act like cowards running away in shame from a lost battle. Because the king is mourning, they fear that doing their duty has actually earned his displeasure.

David covers his face and keeps crying out loud cries of grief for Absalom. Covering the face was a familiar way to express deep, overwhelmed sorrow in the ancient world. Yet continuing this public outburst was driving away the very people who had just risked everything to protect him.

Joab goes into the house to confront David directly, telling him he has brought shame upon his loyal troops. These faithful men had just saved the life of David, his wives, and his children from certain death. Joab reminds the king that public duty must come before private feelings.

Joab bluntly charges David with loving his enemies and hating the people who love him. He points out that the king's actions make the officers and troops feel worthless, as if David would be happier if Absalom lived and all his defenders were dead. Joab's manner is harsh, but his warning addresses a real danger to the kingdom.

Joab urges David to get up, go out, and speak words of encouragement and thanks to his soldiers. He takes a solemn oath that if David refuses, every soldier will abandon him before nightfall. Such a revolt would leave the king in greater ruin than any trial he had ever faced in his life.

David listens to the warning, gets up, and sits in the city gate where the public gathers. Word spreads quickly, and the loyal soldiers come before him to receive his royal thanks and blessing. Meanwhile, the rebellious Israelites who had supported Absalom have scattered back to their own homes.

Across the northern tribes of Israel, the people begin arguing among themselves about what to do next. They remind each other that David had delivered them from the Philistines and many other enemies before Absalom drove him away. With the rebel cause ruined, they begin to remember David's great service to the nation.

The people note that Absalom, whom they chose and anointed to rule over them, has died in battle. They ask why no one is speaking up to bring David back to the throne. His death broke the rebellion, leaving the people eager to restore their rightful king.

David sends word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests to ask the leaders of Judah why they are lagging behind the other tribes. The talk of bringing the king back had spread across Israel, yet Judah remained silent. Because the rebellion started in their territory, Judah's leaders likely held back out of guilt and fear of punishment.

David reminds the elders of Judah that they share his own flesh and blood as his closest tribal relatives. He urges them not to be the last ones to welcome him back. This warm appeal was meant to reassure them that he carried no grudge and was ready to forgive.

David sends a personal promise to Amasa, his nephew who had commanded Absalom's rebel army. He swears that Amasa will replace Joab as commander-in-chief of the royal army. By doing this, David hoped to win the loyalty of the defeated rebels while punishing Joab for killing Absalom.

David's kind words and offer of peace sway the hearts of all the leaders of Judah as if they were one man. United in purpose, they send an official message inviting the king and all his followers to return. David chose to win his people back through grace rather than by force.

David begins his journey back toward Jerusalem and reaches the Jordan River. The leaders of Judah travel to Gilgal on the western bank to meet him and help guide him across. Gilgal was a famous gathering place from early Israelite history, making it a fitting spot to welcome the king home.

Shimei from Bahurim hurries down with the men of Judah to meet King David at the river. When David was fleeing Jerusalem in deep sorrow, Shimei had cursed him and pelted him with stones. Now that David has won, Shimei rushes to ask for mercy before the king takes power again.

Shimei brings a thousand men from the tribe of Benjamin with him to show his standing and plead on his behalf. Ziba, the servant of Saul's family, also rushes to the Jordan along with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. Ziba was eager to get on David's good side before the king discovered his deceit toward Mephibosheth.

A ferry boat crosses the river to carry the king's household across and carry out whatever he desires. Just as David is preparing to cross, Shimei throws himself face down on the ground before the king. He humbles himself completely in front of everyone to beg for his life.

Shimei asks the king not to hold his wrongdoing against him or keep it in his heart. He confesses that his actions on the day David fled Jerusalem were perverse and wicked. He asks David both to forgive his offense and to lay aside any desire for revenge.

Shimei openly acknowledges his guilt and points out that he is the very first person from the northern tribes to welcome the king back. The phrase "house of Joseph" refers to the tribes outside of Judah, which had supported Saul and later Absalom. Shimei hoped that his quick confession and public loyalty would win the king's favor.

Abishai speaks up and demands that Shimei be put to death for cursing the Lord's anointed king. Under God's law, cursing a ruler was a serious crime deserving execution. Abishai believed that a late apology should not spare a dangerous traitor from justice.

David rebukes Abishai and his brother, asking why they are acting like his adversaries on such a joyful day. He refuses to execute anyone, knowing that the Lord has confirmed him as king over all Israel once again. David saw that showing mercy was the best way to heal a divided nation and bring lasting peace.
